newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka Tamil Tiger rebels make strategic attack.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka Tamil Tiger rebels make strategic attack.

text.p: Tamil Tiger separatists hit Sri Lankan troops on Tuesday where they are most vulnerable -- at the rear.

Government forces, in the midst of a major northern offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), were attacked by a large number of rebels early on Tuesday near the government-held frontline town of Vavuniya, some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.

Military analysts said the attack, in which some 500 rebels broke through the military's forward defence line, was expected after recent gains by security forces that had pushed the LTTE into a corner.
They said the rebels would keep looking for weak spots in the military's flanks as troops continued to move north to open a key highway to Jaffna, a further 100 km (60 miles) north of Vavuniya.

The LTTE are fighting an ethnic war, now in its 14th year, for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in mainly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east. The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
Military analysts had predicted a massive diversionary attack on the troops as recently as last week.
They said LTTE's main weapon against the security forces was a surprise attack that would take a heavy toll of men and equipment and at the same time demoralise the troops.
"The aim is to slow down the army and inflict as much damage as possible," said one military analyst.

A huge surprise attack last year by the rebels at an army camp in northeastern Mullaitivu killed several hundred soldiers. The LTTE wiped out the camp and took away a large horde of arms and ammunition.

Casualties in Tuesday's battle, which lasted several hours, were high and included civilians who were caught in the middle as rebels and the troops exchanged artillery and mortar fire. Four civilians died and nearly 30 were wounded at Thandikulam, where the bombardment was centered.
Military officials said three soliders had also died in the battle, but analysts said the toll was likely to increase.

The Defence Ministry said rebels destroyed an ammunition dump in an attempt to disrupt the offensive. Military officials in the north said the LTTE had also blown up a bridge that could hamper troop movements.
Some 20,000 troops launched the latest offensive, code-named "Operation Jaya Sikuru", or "Sure of Victory", on May 13 on two flanks.
The army captured the towns of Omanthai, 14 km (nine miles) north of Vavuniya on one flank, and Nedunkeni, some 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Vavuniya on the other after fierce fighting last month.
The troops are now near the heavily fortified rebel town of Puliyankulam, further north of Omanthai.

Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte said last week that the offensive was aimed at opening the crucial Vavuniya-Jaffna highway through the northern brush-jungle of the Wanni, which is the LTTE heartland.
The highway has been closed for 10 years.
Troops captured the former LTTE stronghold of Jaffna after a major offensive last year, driving the rebels into the Wanni.
Analysts said the biggest headache that the army faced in the current offensive was to guard its rear flanks as troops advanced deeper into the Wanni.
The consolidation of defences in areas taken by the army has been left to other forces -- the navy, air force and police.

But the further the troops advanced, this would extend a rear that has to be manned by other, more inexperienced forces. Military officials say LTTE leaders might be planning more attacks to isolate the advancing troops from their rear support.
Operation Jaya Sikuru could possibly be the last big push by the military against the LTTE, analysts and diplomats have said.
If the army takes the Vavuniya-Jaffna highway it would restrict the Tigers to their jungle lair and cut them off from civilian areas where they recruit fighters, they said.
The rebels, therefore, cannot be expected to give in as easily as they did in February when the military took another crucial highway between Vavuniya and the western coastal town of Mannar.
They said that by opening two simultaneous fronts, the military had ensured that the rebels were spread thinly on the ground and were unable to launch any frontal attacks on the troops.
The only recourse left for the rebels is to mount surprise assaults like the one on Tuesday, they said.
